name: Jade Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that writes appointment software for opticians. I have a two-year college diploma and still ask a senior colleague to check difficult fixes; I prefer a paper test list and have never used an AI tool. I like sorting out a reschedule before a patient gets two reminders. My partner is a school caretaker, our children have grown and moved out, and we have a home loan to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the opticians that the appointment screen still needs a person to check why a patient got two reminders. I write small fixes for our firm's clinic-booking program, and I prefer a printed test list to a new AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, I expect my junior post to carry on. My pay is ordinary for a developer, my partner works full-time as a school caretaker, and we have four months of bills saved, though the home loan still has a few years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing duplicate reminder tickets and comparing them with the clinic's appointment log. Starting next month, we'd cancel the 35 monthly premium channels and put that amount toward the home-loan balance while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this version; two wages and four months saved give us room to pay the loan. I still want the appointment log checked before a reminder goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What caused the two reminders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One patient got a reminder for Tuesday and Thursday because a reschedule left the old slot open. I found the old row and asked the clinic to confirm the correct day before changing the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children live on their own. I would rather talk to our grown children about dinner than ask them to underwrite the home loan.

say: I'd keep **clinic log checks** before sending appointment reminders.
I'd explain **duplicate slots** before buying another software tool.
think: I expect **both wages** and my junior job to hold in a modest AI world.
I have **four months saved**, but the home loan is not finished.
do: Keep **fixing reminder tickets** against the clinic's appointment log.
Cancel **premium channels** and pay 35 extra toward the home loan monthly while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about current wages and the four-month cushion.
S0.quote: I would rather talk to our grown children about dinner than ask them to underwrite the home loan.
fieldNote: **Two wages** and four months saved support calm in the mild case, despite a remaining home loan.
She avoids AI tools and checks **printed clinic records** before changing reminder code.

steps.text: Keep fixing duplicate reminder tickets against clinic appointment log
Pay 35 extra monthly toward loan while both wages hold
Cancel 35 monthly premium channels starting next month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could write the small booking fixes that fill my week, and patients should not learn about errors from a wrong text message. I would want our clinic contact to show me the evidence before anyone changes the reminder schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours because I am still a junior developer at 58. Four months saved gives us a little time, but I am slow with new tools and have never used AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper list of duplicate reminders and bring the actual cases to the weekly release meeting. If the firm cuts junior hours, we'd stop the yearly seaside booking and use its 80 monthly deposit for loan payments while both wages hold; I'd ask my lead about paid vacancies doing clinic testing, but apply only if the wage with my partner's covers the loan and normal bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can catch a bad reminder, but I cannot make the company keep paying me to catch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a reschedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic receptionist marks a reschedule with the patient’s new slot and a crossed-out old one. A neat AI explanation is not a corrected calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which booking would you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seaside booking can wait because we have not paid the final balance. My partner agrees that the home loan comes before a holiday if the firm starts cutting hours.

say: I'd ask for **clinic evidence** before AI changes patient reminders.
I'd say **junior booking fixes** may shrink before my loan ends.
think: I could lose **paid junior hours** while still learning the job.
I have **four months saved**, not a settled retirement income.
do: Keep **paper duplicate-reminder list** and bring real cases to weekly release meetings.
If junior hours are cut, cancel **seaside deposit** and redirect 80 monthly toward the loan while both wages hold.
Ask about **paid clinic-testing vacancies**; apply only if combined wages cover loan and normal bills.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, attached to proof from a clinic log.
S1.quote: A neat AI explanation is not a corrected calendar.
fieldNote: **Small booking fixes** face strong AI change, and her junior standing exposes her own paid hours.
She keeps **paper case evidence** and cuts a planned holiday deposit only if hours fall.

steps.text: Keep logging duplicate reminders and checking clinic cases at weekly release meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that thinking AGI by 2028 can write the reminder code before clinic robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the firm to tell us which posts are ending before the last payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior job could go in that first wave. My partner’s caretaker wage covers some bills but not the loan and everything else. Four months saved is a bridge, not retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask two nearby clinics and the local college about actual paid booking-clerk or test-assistant openings and their wages. If dismissed in the first year after 2028, I'd take a signed post only if its pay with my partner's covers loan, utilities and food; if none qualifies, I'd seek any available paid local work and speak to the lender before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I am not ready to stop earning, and I cannot count a clinic vacancy that has not been advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could show a prospective employer the Tuesday-Thursday reschedule bug with the patient's details removed. It is a small fix, but it shows how I listen to the receptionist rather than trust a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your partner’s hours matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would check whether a job's hours clash with opening the school in the morning. We would reject a supposed fallback that makes my partner lose paid caretaker hours unless the combined pay still covers our bills.

say: I'd ask for **written cut notice** if 2028 thinking AI replaces reminders.
I'd check **real paid openings** before promising a new wage.
think: I expect **my junior post** could go quickly.
I cannot cover **loan and bills** on my partner's wage alone.
do: Ask **two clinics and college** about actual paid booking or test openings and wages now.
After dismissal, take only **signed work** whose combined pay covers loan, utilities and food without losing necessary caretaker pay.
If none qualifies, seek **available paid work** and contact the lender before arrears.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely income loss before retirement is funded.
S2.quote: Four months saved is a bridge, not retirement money.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches reminder code before physical clinic robots around 2031.
Her fallback depends on **signed paid work** and combined wages, including any loss of caretaker hours.

steps.text: Ask two clinics and college about paid booking or test vacancies and wages
Take signed post after dismissal only if combined pay covers loan and bills including caretaker-hour changes
Seek available paid local work if no qualifying clinic post appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 gives me time to learn whether the clinics still pay people to check a changed appointment. Thinking AI arrives then, with physical robots around 2034, but the code is my job first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not want to spend five years pretending my junior post is safe. I have no pension amount in front of me, and I will need wages until a real retirement statement and our loan figures say otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my clinic bug log and request a retirement statement and the loan payoff schedule this winter. I'd ask the clinics for written pay and shift hours for appointment-checking posts; if a real vacancy appears and the wage with my partner's covers loan, utilities and food without clashing with paid caretaker hours, I'd apply and take it after 2031 only on a signed offer, otherwise keep my paid developer work while it exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to check figures rather than an excuse to sit still. I will use a new system if the clinic proves it works, but I will not promise I can master it without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test an AI-generated fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A receptionist can show me a reschedule that a test missed, and I can follow the printed log back to the broken row. I would ask for a paid demonstration before using any AI-generated fix in a live clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two statements tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would put the statement next to the loan schedule. Retiring at 63 is only a date on a birthday card if the income does not cover the payments.

say: I'd ask for **written clinic pay** before leaving development.
I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches booking code before 2034 robots.
think: I cannot assume **five years of wages** or a pension amount.
I need **combined pay** that covers the remaining loan and bills.
do: Keep **clinic bug log** and request retirement and loan statements this winter.
Apply to **real clinic vacancy** only with written hours and combined pay covering bills without losing necessary caretaker pay.
After 2031, move only on **signed offer**; otherwise keep paid developer work while available.
feel: **Anxious** about wages, ready to check documents and proven fixes.
S3.quote: Retiring at 63 is only a date on a birthday card if the income does not cover the payments.
fieldNote: **Retirement figures** and loan balance remain unknown, so five years does not guarantee an affordable exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade until 2036 could take me to 68, but thinking AI will still reach appointment code before clinic robots follow around 2039. I want to know the loan balance before anyone calls me retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have paid off the loan by then or may still need my wage; neither outcome is guaranteed today. Four months saved is helpful now, but it is not a pension and I do not know the retirement amount yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing reminder tickets, redirect the 35 cancelled-channel fee to the loan each month while both wages hold, and check the retirement statement and loan balance once a year. In the first year after 2036 I'd leave paid work only if verified retirement income plus my partner's actual pay covers housing, utilities and food; otherwise I'd keep paid clinic or software work if offered and seek available local shifts if it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a distant change, but the present wages and four-month reserve give us time to do the arithmetic. I am not calling the loan paid until the statement says zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you check each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The yearly statement will have a balance and an end date. I would keep that page with our utility bills, not in a folder called 'someday.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can tell us whether a clinic text is confusing, but their salaries are their own. I would not build a retirement plan around a child's transfer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose my junior wage before another clinic or software employer has a paid opening. Early written notice, vacancy pay in writing and a lender conversation before arrears would help us protect the loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a computer will ever persuade me on its own. A clinic receptionist showing me one correctly fixed appointment would persuade me more than a hundred glowing claims about a new system.

headlineQuote: A clinic receptionist showing me one correctly fixed appointment would persuade me more than a hundred glowing claims about a new system.
portrait: Jade, **58**, is a junior optician-booking developer with a two-year diploma who checks rescheduled appointments against clinic records.
Her **typical wage**, partner's school-caretaker pay, four-month reserve and unfinished home loan make junior-hour cuts a serious risk.
She has **never used AI** and asks for clinic evidence and a paid demonstration before accepting an AI-generated live fix.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; she seeks real signed work only when combined wages cover loan and bills, including caretaker-hour changes.
At a longer horizon, she will **verify retirement income** and loan balance before leaving paid work or assuming help from grown children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior coding wage before a qualifying paid clinic vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Early written notice**, vacancy pay and lender contact before arrears would help protect the home loan.
